newsitem.title: UK: Ford averts British strike threat with union deal.
newsitem.headline: Ford averts British strike threat with union deal.

text.p: U.S. car giant Ford Motor Co averted the threat of a national strike by British workers over job cuts by clinching a deal with trade unions on Friday to secure the future of its Halewood plant in northwest England.
A union statement said the agreement secured jobs and guaranteed job security both at Halewood in Liverpool and throughout the company's other British plants.
Roger Butler of the Amalgamated Engineers and Electricians Unions (AEEU) hailed the breakthrough as "a major victory for Ford workers."

The deal came after two days of talks between Ford's European head Jac Nasser and union leaders. These were a last ditch effort by the workers to try to save 1,300 jobs set to go after Ford's decision last month to move production of its new Escort model to Continental Europe.

Further details of the deal were due to be announced at a joint news conference later on Friday. But unions told reporters the accord meant there would be would be fewer than the 1,300 job losses originally planned at Halewood.
Production of the Escort would still switch to Germany and Spain but union leaders said mainstream models would continue to be made at Halewood.
A threat of a strike by all Ford workers in Britain was called off after the deal, which is expected to be put to a meeting of Halewood workers next week.

Failure of the talks would have resulted in unions calling a strike ballot next week which could have led up to 20,000 Ford production line workers going on strike just ahead of a British election which must be called by May.
Earlier one union official outlined the points put forward to the Ford management in the talks.

"Our arguments are that there is no economic reason for this. The plant has increased productivity, labour costs are down and we have met all our targets. The only reason for moving the jobs to the continent is that the cost of sacking people in Britain is cheaper."
Unions have claimed it is less expensive to cut jobs in Britain because the government has opted out of the European Union's Social Chapter which gives greater protection to employees.

The move to cut jobs was triggered by heavy losses in Ford's European division due to sluggish regional demand, particularly in the French and German markets which make up around 40 percent of Ford's European sales according to industry analyst LMC International.
Ford has in the past held out the prospect of building a new model, possibly a people-carrier van, at Halewood. But that vehicle is still under development and awaiting approval.
The U.S. car giant has also been trying to negotiate an increased subsidy from the British government to secure the future of the plant.
